lesson.title: Drawing the Blueprint Before You Code It
lesson.summary: UML class diagrams are a standard visual notation for sketching a class's attributes, methods, and its relationships to other classes, like inheritance and composition, before or alongside writing the actual code.
lesson.body:
Before writing a class, or when trying to understand a large codebase someone else wrote, it helps to see the shape of the classes involved without reading every line of implementation. UML (Unified Modeling Language) class diagrams are a standard way to draw that shape. Each class is drawn as a box divided into three sections: the class name on top, its attributes in the middle, and its methods on the bottom. A minus sign marks something private, a plus sign marks something public, and each attribute or method is typically followed by its type or return type after a colon.

```
+------------------------+
|         Engine         |
+------------------------+
| - horsepower: int      |
+------------------------+
| + start(): None        |
+------------------------+
```

This box describes an Engine class with one private attribute, horsepower, and one public method, start(), which returns nothing.

Relationships between classes are drawn as lines connecting their boxes, and the shape of the line tells you what kind of relationship it is. An inheritance relationship, the "is-a" relationship from the previous chapter's Dog and Animal example, is drawn as a solid line ending in a hollow, unfilled triangle pointing at the parent class. A composition relationship, where one class is built from, and owns, instances of another, is drawn as a solid line with a filled diamond at the end touching the "whole" class, pointing toward the "part" class it contains. These two lines look deliberately different because they mean genuinely different things: inheritance says "this class is a specialized version of that one," while composition says "this class is made up of, and manages, instances of that one."

Here is a composition relationship, Car "has-a" Engine, alongside the diagram for Car:

```
+------------------------+
|          Car           |
+------------------------+
| - engine: Engine       |
| - fuel: float          |
+------------------------+
| + drive(): None        |
+------------------------+
```

with a filled-diamond line running from the Car box to the Engine box, diamond touching Car, since Car is the whole that contains an Engine as one of its parts. The Python code that implements exactly what this pair of diagrams describes looks like this:

```python
class Engine:
    def __init__(self, horsepower):
        self.horsepower = horsepower

    def start(self):
        print(f"Engine roars to life with {self.horsepower} HP.")

class Car:
    def __init__(self, horsepower, fuel):
        self.engine = Engine(horsepower)
        self.fuel = fuel

    def drive(self):
        self.engine.start()
        print(f"Car drives off with {self.fuel} liters of fuel.")

my_car = Car(300, 40.0)
my_car.drive()
```

This prints:

Engine roars to life with 300 HP.
Car drives off with 40.0 liters of fuel.

Car's __init__ builds a brand new Engine and stores it as self.engine, which is exactly what the diamond-ended composition line in the diagram represents: a Car owns its Engine, creating it and holding onto it, rather than merely referencing one that exists independently elsewhere.

Diagrams like these are a planning and communication tool, not something Python ever reads or executes. Their value is in letting you, or a team, work out how a set of classes should relate before committing to code, and in giving anyone reading the diagram later a fast overview of a hierarchy's shape without opening every file. Several text-based diagramming tools let you describe a class diagram like this one as plain text (an inheritance line and a composition line each get their own distinct notation) and have it rendered as the boxes and connecting lines shown above, which makes it practical to keep a diagram checked in alongside the code it describes.
